cases.note: §18 writes `skynet pair ABCD-1234`. If this case ever stops producing a code, either the alphabet or the length has drifted away from the document’s own example — which is the one string in the specification a user will actually type.
The hyphen is how a code is printed, not part of it. Two spellings of one code must not be two codes.
Nobody holds shift for eight characters, and a code that only worked in upper case would be a support call per robot.
Leading and trailing whitespace from a paste, an inner space where the hyphen was, and a trailing newline. All cosmetic.
Somebody grouping the characters their own way still gets their code. The rule is that hyphens and spaces do not count, not that they appear in one place.

Crockford’s folding, and the reason the alphabet excludes these letters rather than rejecting them: an operator reading `01234567` off a screen types the letters they think they see, and refusing that would be refusing a correct code because a font has a slashed zero.
The worst of the three, because a lower-case l and a 1 are the same glyph in most sans-serif faces. Folded after upper-casing, so `l` and `L` reach the same digit.

The check that exists because an operator holds two secrets at once and will eventually paste the wrong one. Caught before anything is sent, and the refusal names the class rather than the value — a credential echoed into a terminal is a credential in a shell history.

Nothing has been sent. Treat the credential as exposed if it has been on a screen somebody else could see.","position":null}}
